newsitem.title: USA: S.F. Fed's Parry sees risk of inflation pickup.
newsitem.headline: S.F. Fed's Parry sees risk of inflation pickup.

text.p: Robert Parry, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, on Friday said he saw a risk of a rise in inflationary pressures with the economy operating at a high rate of resource utilization.
In prepared remarks to a joint board meeting of Fed bank branches in the Northwest, Parry predicted that the recently strong growth would moderate to a rate of 2.0 to 2.5 percent in the rest of 1996.
"But even with this slowing, it won't be enough to relieve the pressures on our use of resources," he said. "So the potential is there for upward pressure on inflation."
Parry's remarks were largely a repeat of his comments last month at two separate appearances in Portland, Ore. and Cedar City, Utah.

As a sign of the strains on productive resources, Parry referenced the July unemployment rate of 5.4 percent that was reported last month, saying it was a level that "generally has been associated with moderately rising inflation."
Earlier on Friday, the Labor Department released its August employment report showing that the jobless rate dipped to 5.1 percent as the economy created a hefty 250,000 jobs.
In the speech, Parry said structural changes in the economy that appear to have left some workers feeling less secure about their jobs might be a factor in restraining inflation.
"If workers are insecure, they may accept smaller wage increases rather than risk losing the jobs they have," Parry said. "That could help hold down inflation."
On the other hand, he said it is unclear how pervasive the worker insecurity is and whether it will necessarily temper inflation.

"While there is a case that job insecurity is holding inflation down, we just don't have enough evidence to be sure of it," the San Francisco Fed chief said. "Thus, if resource utilization is high, we risk a pickup in inflation."

Parry concluded, "In the period ahead, we must be especially vigilant in monitoring indicators of current and future inflation to guard against losing ground in our effort to move toward price stability."
